Ethos

EE-thoss -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, EE. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Ethos is an appeal to one's morals or ethics.

The company's advertising leans entirely on ethos, promising that it has never sold a product it would not give its own children.

Worked Example

Two speakers argue for the same recycling program. The first cites tonnage figures. The second begins, 'I have picked up litter on this beach every Saturday for eleven years, and I would not stand here asking you for something I was not already doing myself.'

The second speaker is using ethos -- an appeal to her own morals and character, asking the audience to trust her because of who she is and how she lives. Ethos does not prove the claim; it makes the person making the claim worth believing.

How Ethos Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

credibility

credibility: the quality of being believable and trustworthy

character

character: the moral qualities that make up a person

trustworthiness

trustworthiness: the quality of deserving to be relied on

Antonyms

deceit

deceit: lying or tricky behavior that betrays trust

dishonor

dishonor: loss of respect and moral standing

How Strong Is It? — character → ethos → credibility

character vs. ethos

character vs. ethos: Character is what a person actually is; ethos is that character put to work in an argument -- you have character all the time, but you use ethos when you ask an audience to trust you because of it.

credibility vs. ethos

credibility vs. ethos: Credibility is what ethos earns you: a speaker builds ethos by showing her honesty and experience, and the credibility she gains is the reason the audience believes her next sentence.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — ethos

root — ethos: character, habit, the place where one dwells (Greek ethos)

Put it together

Put it together: Ethos is Greek for 'character, habit, the place one lives.' The Greeks saw character as a home a person builds through long habit. In rhetoric, an appeal to ethos asks the audience to look at that home -- the speaker's settled character -- and decide whether to trust the person standing in front of them.

Use the root in a new word: ethical

Use the root in a new word: ethical: The reporter refused the free tickets, because accepting them would not have been ethical.

Root Check

Word Choice

Ethos is one of the three classical rhetorical appeals, alongside Logos (appeals to logic and reason -- taught earlier in this course) and Pathos (appeals to emotion). Ethos, Logos, and Pathos are related but distinct -- they are not synonyms of one another, and a test question will expect you to keep them apart. Ethos is the character appeal: 'trust me, because of who I am.' It also has a second everyday use -- 'the ethos of the school' means the spirit and values of a group.
